extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and patent practitioners who practice before the USPTO; respondents/disciplinary counsel in USPTO OED matters
extracted.subtask_short: USPTO attorney discipline for false declarations
extracted.subtask_description: A USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline Final Order detailing facts, legal conclusions, and sanctions for an attorney's involvement with false Rule 131 patent declarations and related litigation conduct. The page sets out the standards governing truthful submissions to the USPTO, duties in litigation, discovery compliance, and sanctioning considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct standard (elements to prove)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove inequitable conduct, the challenger must show by clear and convincing evidence that the patent applicant (1) misrepresented or omitted information material to patentability, and (2) did so with specific intent to mislead or deceive the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: Therasense v. Becton, Dickinson and Co., 649 F.3d 1276, 1290 (Fed. Cir. 2011), (citing Star Scientific Inc. v. RJ. Reynolds Tobacco Co., 537 F.3d 1357, 1365 (Fed. Cir. 2008)). The page applies this two-part test to declarations that asserted actual reduction to practice when that was false; materiality is shown where the declarations were required to obtain allowance and the examiner relied on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness of Rule 131 declarations submitted to the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations submitted to the USPTO must not contain false statements regarding reduction to practice or other material facts. The document identifies multiple Rule 131 declarations that 'contained false statements relating to reduction to practice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/Findings: original and revised declarations claimed actual reduction to practice, prototypes in the Smithsonian, product brochures and packing receipts, and 'bringing the claimed subject matter to commercialization.' The Federal Circuit and district court found these statements false or obfuscatory and material to allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction and proper representation of constructive vs. actual reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant relies on constructive reduction to practice (i.e., filing date), references to an actual reduction to practice must be removed; statements implying an actual working prototype when only constructive reduction is relied upon are improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The revised declaration in this matter purportedly removed substantive references to actual reduction to practice but left references (e.g., paragraph mentioning a prototype in the Smithsonian) that 'obfuscated the truth' and implied an actual working device. PTO examiners may rely on lingering or ambiguous references as material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty not to file or pursue litigation on patents known or reasonably believed to be procured by false declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney must not file or continue to pursue infringement litigation asserting patents that were procured by false declarations once the attorney knows or should have learned of the falsity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order treats filing complaints (Intellect Wireless v. HTC; Intellect Wireless v. Sharp) when respondents knew or should have known the patents were procured by false declarations as violations of 37 C.F.R. §§10.23(a), 10.23(b)(4), 10.23(b)(5), 10.85(a)(2), and 10.85(a)(3). The Sharp litigation filing after being alerted was found 'objectively unreasonable and vexatious.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to avoid making or repeating false factual allegations in pleadings and discovery responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys should not serve pleadings or interrogatory responses that assert or repeat false statements of fact (e.g., that an inventor built a working prototype or reduced the invention to practice) without a sufficient factual basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples: Second Supplemental Response stated 'there may also be an actual reduction to practice earlier than the date of constructive reduction to practice'; Third Supplemental Response stated 'Mr. Henderson did build a prototype with functional electronics that he believed was an actual reduction to practice' — both were treated as improper where unsupported. Filing Answers that deny counterclaims about false declarations likewise was cited as misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to investigate and to reconcile conflicting information once alerted to potential falsity
rubrics_metrics.description: When counsel is informed or reasonably should be aware of information contradicting prior sworn statements (e.g., client emails admitting the device 'did not operate'), counsel must investigate and reconcile those facts before repeating or amplifying the prior assertions in court filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record shows counsel received an email on Nov. 6, 2009 admitting the prototype did not operate and was a mock-up. HTC counsel alerted Respondent Sept. 23, 2010 that declarations were false. The failure to reconcile the November 6, 2009 email with the declarations before filing the Sharp litigation was found 'objectively unreasonable and vexatious.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on unreasonably multiplying proceedings (28 U.S.C. § 1927 / professional conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys must not unreasonably and vexatiously multiply proceedings in litigation; doing so can lead to civil liability for attorneys' fees and disciplinary violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts found that filing an amended complaint repeating misleading allegations and pursuing claims on an unenforceable patent 'unnecessarily multiplied these proceedings' and ordered liability under 28 U.S.C. § 1927. The Final Order cites violations of 37 C.F.R. §§10.23(a), 10.23(b)(5), and 10.85(a)(2) tied to such conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to comply with court orders and discovery; failure can support adverse inferences and sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsel must comply with discovery orders and produce requested documents; failure to do so can result in motions to compel, orders requiring production, adverse inference findings, and sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chronology: motions for expedited discovery, orders to produce, a motion to compel, and an adverse inference were granted — the district court concluded counsel's failure to comply supported an adverse inference that they knew the declarations were false prior to litigation. Noncompliance contributed to findings of sanctionable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to correct the record with the USPTO when false or misleading statements have been made
rubrics_metrics.description: When false statements have been presented to the USPTO, a full disclosure or correction of the record should be made; failure to do so is actionable and material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The district court found that a full disclosure or correction of the record was never made, and that examiners relied on the declarations. The Final Order emphasizes that the revised declaration failed to correct the falsehoods and in some respects 'danced around the truth.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on making statements that imply commercialization or existence of a working product when none exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that a product was 'brought to commercialization', that a prototype 'is now in the Smithsonian', or that there are product brochures/packing receipts when no functioning product existed are misleading and material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit found the revised declaration's references to commercialization, a Smithsonian prototype, and product materials implied an actual working device 'even though there was no product' and contributed to a conclusion of intent to deceive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific USPTO Rules and regulatory provisions implicated by such conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The Final Order identifies violations of specific USPTO rules: 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(a), 10.23(b)(4), 10.23(b)(5), 10.85(a)(2), 10.85(a)(3), 11.804(i), and 10.23(b)(6) in connection with filing claims, serving interrogatory responses, multiplying proceedings, and other conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order ties particular acts to these rule citations (e.g., filing complaints while aware of false declarations; serving responses asserting actual reduction to practice; unreasonably multiplying proceedings). Practitioners should consult the text of these sections for the exact regulatory requirements and prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations for sanctions and mitigating/aggravating factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions are determined considering both culpability and mitigating factors such as status in firm, reliance on senior counsel or experts, good faith beliefs, and cooperation; the agreed-upon sanction here was an 18-month suspension and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order lists miscellaneous factors: Respondent was the most junior attorney, relied in good faith on senior lawyers and client statements, and the firm obtained an expert advising the basis was constructive reduction to practice. Nonetheless, Respondent acknowledged seriousness of false/misleading statements. Agreed sanctions: 18-month suspension from practice before the USPTO in patent/trademark/non-patent matters, compliance with 37 C.F.R. §§11.58 and 11.59, publication in OED Reading Room and the Official Gazette, and that the record may be considered in future proceedings as aggravation.
